Emma's Mom Hacks
Sponsored
My son (26mo) potty trained in 3 days, while his older sister took almost a year. Here's what we did differently...

Because when I look back at that year with my daughter, I realize I made it SO much harder than it needed to be.

With my first, I was understandably a little arrogant. I thought "how hard can it be?"

I'd seen so many moms online do it in a weekend. Heck, there's even a method called "3 day potty training."

Oh boy was I wrong....

---

I bought the cute potty. I bought the sticker charts. And I stocked up on disposables because I HATE changing diapers and didn't want pee on my rugs.

And that was the decision that wasted nearly a year of our lives.

For nearly 11 months, my daughter treated those disposables exactly like diapers. She would look me dead in the eye, pee, and keep playing.

I’d ask "Did you just go?" and she’d say "No."

And I thought she was lying straight to my face.

I spent months begging, bribing, and pleading for her to sit on the potty.

I thought she was stubborn. I thought she "wasn't ready." I thought I was failing her.

She did eventually get it. One day she just decided she wanted to use the toilet. Like... Excuse me??? 

All this time just for you to decide?? 🤦🤦🤦

So when my son turned 2, I felt dread. Not excitement. Dread.

I looked at my husband and said: "I cannot go through this again with him."

--

So I was doom-scrolling Instagram one night, trying to unwind.

And I found a Reel from a Pediatric Occupational Therapist explaining the "Sensory Loop."

She asked a question that stopped me in my tracks: "How can you teach a child to control a sensation they literally cannot feel?"

She explained that modern diapers and disposables are engineering marvels. They absorb moisture so fast that the skin stays perfectly dry.

And that's when it hit me. That’s why my daughter said "No" when I asked if she was wet. She wasn't lying. She genuinely didn't feel it.

The OT said: "You are trying to teach them to control a bladder they are deaf to."

She said the solution is to remove the disposables immediately.

BUT... she said do not use regular underwear either. Because while underwear helps them feel wet, it creates huge puddles on your floor. 

And cleaning up accidents 5 times a day creates stress, which makes the child shut down.

So you are stuck: 
Disposables = No Feeling (No Learning). 
Underwear = Huge Mess (High Stress).

She said you need a hybrid - "Training Pants."

She recommended UpAiry training pants.

She said they have a specific technology that stays wet against the skin for just long enough to send a "signal" to the brain. It creates a sensory "Cause and Effect."

Pee = Wet. Wet = Yuck.

But the outer layer locks it in so it doesn't leak everywhere.

She also said this is why the last generation (our parents) never had the issues we have. They all used cloth diapers where the toddler COULD feel their mess.

She said she'd tried a few other brands out there but the UpAiry ones were the best she'd used.

It sounded too simple, but the logic made sense. So I ordered them.

I put them on my son (who is only 26 months). I didn't explain anything. I didn't do a sticker chart. I just let him play.

--

Day 1: He peed. He stopped playing immediately and walked funny. 

He looked down with wide eyes. "Wet." He felt it. The connection was instant. 

With my daughter, it took 6 months for her to even notice she was peeing.

Day 2: He started to go, felt the dampness, and ran to the potty to finish. He realized he could STOP the "yuck" feeling by using the potty.

Day 3: He was dry all day. He went to the potty every time he felt the urge.

THREE. DAYS.

I looked at my husband and said, "Are you kidding me? We struggled for a YEAR with his sister, and it was just the underwear the whole time?"

My husband said, "Well, at least we figured it out eventually."

--

Also!!! My sister-in-law is currently training her 3-year-old and was having the EXACT same struggle I had with my daughter. Accidents, apathy, "I don't care."

I sent her the link to the training pants we used and said "let the training pants teach him what the urge feels like."

She texted me 5 days later: "He just pooped in the potty for the first time. I am literally crying."

It wasn't that our kids were stubborn. It wasn't that they "weren't ready." It was just that they couldn't feel the signal.

So if you are struggling with a toddler who just doesn't seem to care. Don't make the same mistake I made with my first.

Hope this saves another mom a year of stress (and money on disposables).

EDIT: Getting a lot of DMs asking which ones we used for my son. I thought I mentioned it but here is the link: https://www.upairy.com/pages/training-underwear

This page explains the everything way better than I can.

Sponsored
My 4-year-old is still in diapers.

And I genuinely don't understand why.

My name is Bec I'm 31 years old.

And for two years, I've been trying to figure out why my daughter won't potty train.

Not "won't try."

Won't train.

She's smart. She can read some words. She knows her numbers. 

She follows instructions perfectly.

But potty training? Nothing sticks.

And the confusing part is her younger brother trained at 2 and a half.

No issues. No drama. He just got it.

So what's different?

We first tried when she was 2 and a half.

I read the books. Did the 3-day method. Set aside a long weekend.

Day one was rough. Lots of accidents. But I expected that.

Day two, she seemed to be getting it.

Day three, complete shutdown.

Refused the potty. Held her pee for five hours. Had a meltdown.

I figured okay, she's not ready yet. We'll try again in a few months.

We tried again at 3.

Same pattern. A few days of progress, then total resistance.

Back to diapers.

Tried again at 3 and a half. Same thing.

Every time, it was like hitting a wall.

She'd make a little progress. Then something would shut down. She'd refuse. We'd stop.

I talked to her pediatrician.

She said some kids are more resistant. 

To keep trying.

Stay consistent.

I talked to other moms.

They said maybe she's stubborn. Maybe she needs different rewards. Maybe she has a fear.

I tried everything they suggested.

Different rewards. Special potty seats. Songs. Books. Stickers. Screen time.

Nothing worked.

And then her little brother started showing interest.

He was 2 and a half. Watching her sit on the potty sometimes.

One day he asked to try.

He went. Just like that.

Two weeks later, he was trained.

No meltdowns. No resistance. He just figured it out.

And my daughter? Still in diapers.

I kept thinking there had to be a reason.

She wasn't being stubborn for no reason.

Kids don't refuse to learn something for two years just because.

There had to be something I was missing.

Last spring, I tried to enroll her in preschool.

Great program. Small classes. Everything I wanted.

Two weeks before she was supposed to start, the director sent an email.

"All children must be fully potty trained before the first day."

I called and asked if there was flexibility.

She said no. Health code issue. We could try again in the fall.

I was frustrated, but I understood.

So we had the summer. Plenty of time to figure this out.

I decided to really research this. 

Not just tips and tricks.

But why.

Why would one kid train easily and another resist for years?

That's when I found a video from a child psychologist talking about prolonged potty training resistance.

She said something that made me stop.

"When toddlers resist training for years, parents assume it's behavioral. But it's almost never behavioral. It's sensory."

She explained that most kids who can't train after years of trying aren't refusing to learn.

They literally can't feel the signals.

When you wear diapers for years, your brain learns to tune out the sensation of peeing.

It becomes background noise. 

Something your brain stops paying attention to.

So when you ask a 4-year-old to "tell me when you need to go," they genuinely don't know.

Because they've spent four years in something that instantly absorbs everything.

They've never felt wet. Never felt uncomfortable.

Their brain learned to ignore that sensation completely.

This is why switching to pull-ups doesn't help.

Pull-ups absorb just as fast. They feel the same to the brain.

So the signal stays blocked.

And this is why older toddlers resist so hard.

They're being asked to notice something they've been trained to ignore.

Think of it like this.

We learn through cause and effect.

Touch hot stove -> Ouch, don't do again

Same thing applies here.

Their brain has no idea they have peed, they can't feel it

About how she'd say "I don't need to go" and then have an accident five minutes later.

She wasn't lying. She genuinely didn't feel it.

About how her brother trained so easily at 2 and a half.

He'd only been in diapers for two and a half years. 

His brain hadn't tuned it out yet.

But my daughter? Four years of diapers. Four years of her brain learning to ignore that signal.

No wonder nothing was working.

I wasn't asking her to learn something new.

I was asking her to unlearn four years of ignoring her body.

The next morning, I told my husband what I'd learned.

He said "that actually makes sense. So what do we do?"

I said we need to stop using diapers completely. And pull-ups won't work either.

We need something that creates strong enough sensory feedback that her brain can't ignore it.

He said "so just let her have accidents everywhere?"

I said no. There are training pants designed specifically for this.

Real training pants that let kids feel wetness but contain it.

I started looking.

Most training pants were either crap quality or not absorbent enough (complete mess).

But I kept seeing parents of older toddlers mention UpAiry training pants.

They said these had Feel & Learn technology. Strong sensory feedback but no leaking.

I read reviews from parents of 3, 4, even 5-year-olds who'd been stuck for years.

Same story over and over.

"My child couldn't feel anything in pull-ups."

"Once she could actually feel it, she got it in days."

"I didn't realize diapers had trained her brain to ignore the signal."

I was skeptical. We'd tried so many things.

But the science made sense.

And they had a 75-day guarantee.

After two years, I figured why not.

I ordered them.

When they arrived, I put them on my daughter.

"These are your new underwear. They work differently."

The first day, she had six accidents.

But something happened that never happened before.

Every single time, she stopped immediately.

"Mommy, it's happening."

Not "I went." Not "I'm wet."

"It's happening."

Present tense.

She could feel it while it was happening.

In four years, she'd never felt that.

Day two, five accidents. All announced as they happened.

Day three, she was playing. Stopped. Grabbed her stomach.

"Mommy, I feel something."

We ran to the bathroom. She went.

She looked amazed. "I felt it before!"

Week one, she started telling me before accidents.

Her brain was finally learning to recognize the signal.

Week two, she was making it to the potty most of the time.

Week three, two accidents all week.

My husband said "I can't believe the difference."

I said "she just needed to actually feel it."

Month two, she's been completely dry for three weeks.

Tells me when she needs to go. Takes herself sometimes.

Last week, I called the preschool. Asked about fall enrollment.

They said yes, there's still space.

She starts in the next few months.

Yesterday, she was playing outside with neighborhood kids.

Came inside once to use the bathroom. Went right back out.

No accidents. No issues.

On the way to bed, she said "I'm glad I learned."

And I realized something.

For two years, I thought she was resisting.

That something was wrong with her approach or my approach.

But she wasn't resisting anything.

Her brain just couldn't hear the signal.

And once I gave her something that created a signal strong enough to break through, she learned in weeks.

Look, if you have an older toddler who's been stuck for months or years, and nothing you've tried has worked, this might be why.

It's not behavioral. It's not stubbornness.

Years in diapers or pull-ups train the brain to tune out elimination signals.

You can try every method. Every reward. Every trick.

But if their brain can't hear the signal, they can't learn.

I spent two years trying everything except the one thing that actually mattered.

Sensory feedback.

These training pants worked because they create feedback strong enough that the brain can't ignore it anymore.

Not magic. Just science.

Here's the link if you want to check them out: https://www.upairy.com/pages/training-underwear

I'm not affiliated with them. 

Just a mom who finally figured out what was blocking progress.

My daughter's not in diapers anymore.

She's not stuck anymore.

And it only took weeks once we addressed the actual problem.

You don't need another method.

You need sensory feedback.

That's what finally worked.

I've worked in early childhood education for 11 years.

I've helped potty train hundreds of kids across three different daycares.

And I can tell you something that most parenting books won't.

I can predict within the first week which kids are going to train fast and which ones are going to struggle for months.

It has nothing to do with the child's intelligence. 

It has nothing to do with their personality. 

And it has very little to do with the parents approach.

It has to do with one thing. 

And once I explain it, you'll probably look at your own child's situation completely differently.

—

Let me back up.

When I first started working in childcare, I assumed potty training was mostly about timing and temperament.

Some kids were ready at 2. Some weren't ready until 3 or later. Some were stubborn. Some were easygoing.

And for the first few years, I didn't question it.

But somewhere around year three or four, I started noticing a pattern that I couldn't explain.

We'd get a class of ten toddlers starting the potty training transition around the same age.

And without fail, the class would split into two groups.

Group one would show potty awareness pretty quick, and group two don't have a care in the world

You could ask them "did you just go?" and they'd say no.

Genuinely. 

They weren't lying and they weren't being difficult.

They had no idea.

And this group would struggle for months. Sometimes half a year. Sometimes longer.

I kept thinking it had to be a personality thing. Some kids just develop that awareness later.

But it wasn't consistent. I'd see a kid who was sharp as anything, sit in a wet pull-up for an hour without noticing. 

And I'd see a kid who was still barely talking, walk himself to the potty at 22 months like it was nothing.

It didn't track with development. It didn't track with temperament. It didn't track with anything I'd been trained on.

But it DID track with one thing.

What they were wearing when they arrived.

—

It took me years to put this together because I wasn't looking for it.
But once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it.

The kids who trained fast almost always came in wearing either cloth-style training pants or thin cotton underwear from day one.

The kids who struggled for months were almost always in disposables/diapers

Every. Single. Time.

I started paying closer attention. Not just to the kids in my class but across the entire center.

Same pattern.

Pull-ups and disposables = months of issues and zero awareness.

Cloth or cotton training pants = fast awareness and trained within weeks.

I brought this up to the center director once. 

She said "well yeah, kids in underwear feel it when they go, so they learn faster."

And I remember thinking... that's it? That's the whole thing?

Because if that's the whole thing, then why is everyone still putting their kids in disposables?

Why are we recommending them in our parent packets? 

If the thing they're wearing is the thing blocking the awareness, then aren't we actively making it harder?

—

There was a little girl in my class a couple years ago. I'm going to call her Sophie.

Sophie was 3 and a half. Smart. Social. One of the most verbal kids in the room. 

She could tell you about her weekend in full sentences. She knew every kid's name, every teacher's name.

But she could not potty train.

Her mom had been trying since Sophie turned 2. 

She was stressed. 

She'd pull me aside at least once a week.

"Any progress today?"

And I'd have to tell her no. Sophie had three, four, five accidents a day. 

I'd often walk over and say "Sophie, I think you might be wet."

She'd look at me confused. Then look down. Then say "Oh."

This went on for months.

Her mom tried everything. 

She brought special treats for rewards, every method and thing you've probably done yourself

Nothing changed.

Seeing Sophie say "I didn't go" when she obviously had.

And I kept thinking about the pattern I'd been seeing for years.

Sophie was in disposables every single day. 

Thick, absorbent, dry to the touch within seconds.

And she had zero awareness of her own body.

I've worked in early childhood education for 11 years.

I've helped potty train hundreds of kids across three different daycares.

And I can tell you something that most parenting books won't.

I can predict within the first week which kids are going to train fast and which ones are going to struggle for months.

It has nothing to do with the child's intelligence. 

It has nothing to do with their personality. 

And it has very little to do with the parents approach.

It has to do with one thing. 

And once I explain it, you'll probably look at your own child's situation completely differently.

—

Let me back up.

When I first started working in childcare, I assumed potty training was mostly about timing and temperament.

Some kids were ready at 2. Some weren't ready until 3 or later. Some were stubborn. Some were easygoing.

And for the first few years, I didn't question it.

But somewhere around year three or four, I started noticing a pattern that I couldn't explain.

We'd get a class of ten toddlers starting the potty training transition around the same age.

And without fail, the class would split into two groups.

Group one would show potty awareness pretty quick, and group two don't have a care in the world

You could ask them "did you just go?" and they'd say no.

Genuinely. 

They weren't lying and they weren't being difficult.

They had no idea.

And this group would struggle for months. Sometimes half a year. Sometimes longer.

I kept thinking it had to be a personality thing. Some kids just develop that awareness later.

But it wasn't consistent. I'd see a kid who was sharp as anything, sit in a wet pull-up for an hour without noticing. 

And I'd see a kid who was still barely talking, walk himself to the potty at 22 months like it was nothing.

It didn't track with development. It didn't track with temperament. It didn't track with anything I'd been trained on.

But it DID track with one thing.

What they were wearing when they arrived.

—

It took me years to put this together because I wasn't looking for it.
But once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it.

The kids who trained fast almost always came in wearing either cloth-style training pants or thin cotton underwear from day one.

The kids who struggled for months were almost always in disposables/diapers

Every. Single. Time.

I started paying closer attention. Not just to the kids in my class but across the entire center.

Same pattern.

Pull-ups and disposables = months of issues and zero awareness.

Cloth or cotton training pants = fast awareness and trained within weeks.

I brought this up to the center director once. 

She said "well yeah, kids in underwear feel it when they go, so they learn faster."

And I remember thinking... that's it? That's the whole thing?

Because if that's the whole thing, then why is everyone still putting their kids in disposables?

Why are we recommending them in our parent packets? 

If the thing they're wearing is the thing blocking the awareness, then aren't we actively making it harder?

—

There was a little girl in my class a couple years ago. I'm going to call her Sophie.

Sophie was 3 and a half. Smart. Social. One of the most verbal kids in the room. 

She could tell you about her weekend in full sentences. She knew every kid's name, every teacher's name.

But she could not potty train.

Her mom had been trying since Sophie turned 2. 

She was stressed. 

She'd pull me aside at least once a week.

"Any progress today?"

And I'd have to tell her no. Sophie had three, four, five accidents a day. 

I'd often walk over and say "Sophie, I think you might be wet."

She'd look at me confused. Then look down. Then say "Oh."

This went on for months.

Her mom tried everything. 

She brought special treats for rewards, every method and thing you've probably done yourself

Nothing changed.

Seeing Sophie say "I didn't go" when she obviously had.

And I kept thinking about the pattern I'd been seeing for years.

Sophie was in disposables every single day. 

Thick, absorbent, dry to the touch within seconds.

And she had zero awareness of her own body.

Those two things weren't a coincidence.

—

Around this same time, I started reading more about child development in toddlers. 

Not just the daycare training manual stuff — actual research.

There's a concept in child development called sensory filtering. 

It's the brain's ability to tune out repeated sensations so they don't distract you.

It's the same reason you stop noticing the feeling of your shirt on your skin after you put it on. 

Your brain filters it out. 

It's not useful information anymore so your brain stops paying attention to it.

When a baby pees in a diaper, the diaper absorbs it instantly. The skin stays dry. 

The brain gets no feedback.

So the brain learns: this sensation is irrelevant. Filter it out.

At 18 months, the filter is still weak. 

Most kids can still feel the signal if you take the diaper off.

That's why early training often works quickly.

But by 2 and a half, 3, 3 and a half — the filter is strong. Years of the brain practicing ignoring a signal that never produced any feedback.

Parents often put these kids in a classroom and ask them to tell us when they need to go.

But their brain is filtering the signal.

That's why Sophie would say "I didn't go" and genuinely mean it. 

Her brain had spent three and a half years erasing the sensation.

It wasn't anyones fault.

It was the product she'd been wearing since birth doing exactly what it was designed to do - keep her dry. 

This is also why our parents' generation trained earlier. In the 1950s, 92% of children trained by 18 months. 

Cloth diapers stayed wet. The brain always got the signal. The filter never built up.

Disposables removed the signal. The average training age nearly doubled.

And once I understood this, the pattern I'd been watching for years finally had a name.

Sensory erasure.

—

So here's what I did with Sophie.

I talked to her mom at pickup one day and told her everything I'd been observing.

I told her about the two groups I see and what they're wearing being the only consistent difference.

I told her about how the disposable were erasing the signal Sophie's brain needed to learn.

And I told her that she needed to get Sophie out of disposables and into training pants.

Real training pants. The kind that let the child feel wetness against the skin but contain it so there's no puddle on the floor.

She asked me which ones.

I told her the ones I'd seen work best with the kids in our center were UpAiry training pants. 

They have special layer that holds wetness against the skin long enough for the brain to register it, but the outer layer catches everything.

I'd seen other parents bring in different brands. 

Some leaked. 

Some were cheap polyester that irritated kids' skin.

The UpAiry ones were the only ones I'd consistently seen produce that awareness shift in the first few days.

She ordered them that night.

—

The next Monday, Sophie came in wearing them.

Around 10 AM she was at the art table painting. And she stopped. Brush in the air. Looked down.

"Miss? Pee pee."

Three and a half years old. Months in my classroom. She had NEVER said that. Not once.

I walked over and said "You're right, you are. Let's go get changed."

She looked at me and said "I didn't want to be wet."

She FELT something. And she didn't like it. And she told me about it.

That is the entire learning loop. 

Feel it → don't like it → communicate it → eventually learn to prevent it.

By the end of the first week, she was walking to the bathroom before most accidents. Not every time. But most.

Her mom came in on Friday and I said "She's telling us before she goes now."

She just stood there in the doorway. 

Didn't say anything for a second. Then said "Are you serious?"

Week two, Sophie was using the bathroom independently. 

Raising her hand, walking over, going. Coming back to the table.

Week three, not a single accident for three straight days. 

I wrote it in her daily report and her mom was SO happy 

She said "I've been trying for a year and a half. Thank you for telling me what was actually wrong."

But I didn't do anything special. 

Sophie did it by herself. 

All we did was stop blocking the signal it needed.

—

That was two years ago.

Since then I've had this same conversation with probably fifty parents. Maybe more.

It's always the same situation. Kid has been struggling for months. Parent has tried everything.

And every time I ask the same question: "What are they wearing during the day?"

And every time the answer is some sort of disposable.

And every time I explain what they are actually doing to the learning process and recommend they switch to UpAiry.

And almost every time, the parent comes back telling me things are finally clicking.

Because their child's brain finally had something to learn from.

—

Here's what I tell every parent who walks into my classroom.

If your child is 2 and a half or older and potty training isn't progressing, the first thing I'd look at is what they're wearing.

If they're in disposables during the day, their brain may not be getting the sensory feedback it needs to build awareness. 

Get them into training pants that let them feel wetness but contain it. 

That's the bridge between diapers and underwear that most parents skip.

The ones I've seen work consistently are UpAiry training pants. 

Here's the link: https://www.upairy.com/pages/training-underwear

I have zero affiliation with them. I just see what works in my classroom every day.

In 11 years I've watched hundreds of kids go through this. 

The pattern is always the same.

Sensory feedback = fast learning.

Sensory erasure = months of frustration.

It really is that simple. 

I wish someone had explained it to me in my first year instead of my eleventh.

It would have saved a lot of parents a lot of hard months.

Here's what we did differently...

Because when I look back at that year with my daughter, I realize I made it SO much harder than it needed to be.

With my first, I was understandably a little arrogant. I thought "how hard can it be?"

I'd seen so many moms online do it in a weekend. Heck, there's even a method called "3 day potty training."

Oh boy was I wrong....

---

I bought the cute potty. I bought the sticker charts. And I stocked up on disposables because I HATE changing diapers and didn't want pee on my rugs.

And that was the decision that wasted nearly a year of our lives.

For nearly 11 months, my daughter treated those disposables exactly like diapers. She would look me dead in the eye, pee, and keep playing.

I’d ask "Did you just go?" and she’d say "No."

And I thought she was lying straight to my face.

I spent months begging, bribing, and pleading for her to sit on the potty.

I thought she was stubborn. I thought she "wasn't ready." I thought I was failing her.

She did eventually get it. One day she just decided she wanted to use the toilet. Like... Excuse me??? 

All this time just for you to decide?? 🤦🤦🤦

So when my son turned 2, I felt dread. Not excitement. Dread.

I looked at my husband and said: "I cannot go through this again with him."

--

So I was doom-scrolling Instagram one night, trying to unwind.

And I found a Reel from a Pediatric Occupational Therapist explaining the "Sensory Loop."

She asked a question that stopped me in my tracks: "How can you teach a child to control a sensation they literally cannot feel?"

She explained that modern diapers and disposables are engineering marvels. They absorb moisture so fast that the skin stays perfectly dry.

And that's when it hit me. That’s why my daughter said "No" when I asked if she was wet. She wasn't lying. She genuinely didn't feel it.

The OT said: "You are trying to teach them to control a bladder they are deaf to."

She said the solution is to remove the disposables immediately.

BUT... she said do not use regular underwear either. Because while underwear helps them feel wet, it creates huge puddles on your floor. 

And cleaning up accidents 5 times a day creates stress, which makes the child shut down.

So you are stuck: 
Disposables = No Feeling (No Learning). 
Underwear = Huge Mess (High Stress).

She said you need a hybrid - "Training Pants."

She recommended UpAiry training pants.

She said they have a specific technology that stays wet against the skin for just long enough to send a "signal" to the brain. It creates a sensory "Cause and Effect."

Pee = Wet. Wet = Yuck.

But the outer layer locks it in so it doesn't leak everywhere.

She also said this is why the last generation (our parents) never had the issues we have. They all used cloth diapers where the toddler COULD feel their mess.

She said she'd tried a few other brands out there but the UpAiry ones were the best she'd used.

It sounded too simple, but the logic made sense. So I ordered them.

I put them on my son (who is only 26 months). I didn't explain anything. I didn't do a sticker chart. I just let him play.

--

Day 1: He peed. He stopped playing immediately and walked funny. 

He looked down with wide eyes. "Wet." He felt it. The connection was instant. 

With my daughter, it took 6 months for her to even notice she was peeing.

Day 2: He started to go, felt the dampness, and ran to the potty to finish. He realized he could STOP the "yuck" feeling by using the potty.

Day 3: He was dry all day. He went to the potty every time he felt the urge.

THREE. DAYS.

I looked at my husband and said, "Are you kidding me? We struggled for a YEAR with his sister, and it was just the underwear the whole time?"

My husband said, "Well, at least we figured it out eventually."

--

Also!!! My sister-in-law is currently training her 3-year-old and was having the EXACT same struggle I had with my daughter. Accidents, apathy, "I don't care."

I sent her the link to the training pants we used and said "let the training pants teach him what the urge feels like."

She texted me 5 days later: "He just pooped in the potty for the first time. I am literally crying."

It wasn't that our kids were stubborn. It wasn't that they "weren't ready." It was just that they couldn't feel the signal.

So if you are struggling with a toddler who just doesn't seem to care. Don't make the same mistake I made with my first.

Hope this saves another mom a year of stress (and money on disposables).

I spent months begging, bribing, and pleading for her to sit on the potty.

I thought she was stubborn. I thought she "wasn't ready." I thought I was failing her.

She did eventually get it. One day she just decided she wanted to use the toilet. Like... Excuse me??? 

All this time just for you to decide?? 🤦🤦🤦

So when my son turned 2, I felt dread. Not excitement. Dread.

I looked at my husband and said: "I cannot go through this again with him."

--

So I was doom-scrolling Instagram one night, trying to unwind.

And I found a Reel from a Pediatric Occupational Therapist explaining the "Sensory Loop."

She asked a question that stopped me in my tracks: "How can you teach a child to control a sensation they literally cannot feel?"

She explained that modern diapers and disposables are engineering marvels. They absorb moisture so fast that the skin stays perfectly dry.

And that's when it hit me. That’s why my daughter said "No" when I asked if she was wet. She wasn't lying. She genuinely didn't feel it.

The OT said: "You are trying to teach them to control a bladder they are deaf to."

She said the solution is to remove the disposables immediately.

BUT... she said do not use regular underwear either. Because while underwear helps them feel wet, it creates huge puddles on your floor. 

And cleaning up accidents 5 times a day creates stress, which makes the child shut down.

So you are stuck: 
Disposables = No Feeling (No Learning). 
Underwear = Huge Mess (High Stress).

She said you need a hybrid - "Training Pants."

She recommended UpAiry training pants.

She said they have a specific technology that stays wet against the skin for just long enough to send a "signal" to the brain. It creates a sensory "Cause and Effect."

Pee = Wet. Wet = Yuck.

But the outer layer locks it in so it doesn't leak everywhere.

She also said this is why the last generation (our parents) never had the issues we have. They all used cloth diapers where the toddler COULD feel their mess.

She said she'd tried a few other brands out there but the UpAiry ones were the best she'd used.

It sounded too simple, but the logic made sense. So I ordered them.

I put them on my son (who is only 26 months). I didn't explain anything. I didn't do a sticker chart. I just let him play.

--

Day 1: He peed. He stopped playing immediately and walked funny. 

He looked down with wide eyes. "Wet." He felt it. The connection was instant. 

With my daughter, it took 6 months for her to even notice she was peeing.

Day 2: He started to go, felt the dampness, and ran to the potty to finish. He realized he could STOP the "yuck" feeling by using the potty.

Day 3: He was dry all day. He went to the potty every time he felt the urge.

THREE. DAYS.

I looked at my husband and said, "Are you kidding me? We struggled for a YEAR with his sister, and it was just the underwear the whole time?"

My husband said, "Well, at least we figured it out eventually."

--

Also!!! My sister-in-law is currently training her 3-year-old and was having the EXACT same struggle I had with my daughter. Accidents, apathy, "I don't care."

I sent her the link to the training pants we used and said "let the training pants teach him what the urge feels like."

She texted me 5 days later: "He just pooped in the potty for the first time. I am literally crying."

It wasn't that our kids were stubborn. It wasn't that they "weren't ready." It was just that they couldn't feel the signal.

So if you are struggling with a toddler who just doesn't seem to care. Don't make the same mistake I made with my first.

Hope this saves another mom a year of stress (and money on disposables).

And I genuinely don't understand why.

My name is Bec I'm 31 years old.

And for two years, I've been trying to figure out why my daughter won't potty train.

Not "won't try."

Won't train.

She's smart. She can read some words. She knows her numbers. 

She follows instructions perfectly.

But potty training? Nothing sticks.

And the confusing part is her younger brother trained at 2 and a half.

No issues. No drama. He just got it.

So what's different?

We first tried when she was 2 and a half.

I read the books. Did the 3-day method. Set aside a long weekend.

Day one was rough. Lots of accidents. But I expected that.

Day two, she seemed to be getting it.

Day three, complete shutdown.

Refused the potty. Held her pee for five hours. Had a meltdown.

I figured okay, she's not ready yet. We'll try again in a few months.

We tried again at 3.

Same pattern. A few days of progress, then total resistance.

Back to diapers.

Tried again at 3 and a half. Same thing.

Every time, it was like hitting a wall.

She'd make a little progress. Then something would shut down. She'd refuse. We'd stop.

I talked to her pediatrician.

She said some kids are more resistant. 

To keep trying.

Stay consistent.

I talked to other moms.

They said maybe she's stubborn. Maybe she needs different rewards. Maybe she has a fear.

I tried everything they suggested.

Different rewards. Special potty seats. Songs. Books. Stickers. Screen time.

Nothing worked.

And then her little brother started showing interest.

He was 2 and a half. Watching her sit on the potty sometimes.

One day he asked to try.

He went. Just like that.

Two weeks later, he was trained.

No meltdowns. No resistance. He just figured it out.

And my daughter? Still in diapers.

I kept thinking there had to be a reason.

She wasn't being stubborn for no reason.

Kids don't refuse to learn something for two years just because.

There had to be something I was missing.

Last spring, I tried to enroll her in preschool.

Great program. Small classes. Everything I wanted.

Two weeks before she was supposed to start, the director sent an email.

"All children must be fully potty trained before the first day."

I called and asked if there was flexibility.

She said no. Health code issue. We could try again in the fall.

I was frustrated, but I understood.

So we had the summer. Plenty of time to figure this out.

I decided to really research this. 

Not just tips and tricks.

But why.

Why would one kid train easily and another resist for years?

That's when I found a video from a child psychologist talking about prolonged potty training resistance.

She said something that made me stop.

"When toddlers resist training for years, parents assume it's behavioral. But it's almost never behavioral. It's sensory."

She explained that most kids who can't train after years of trying aren't refusing to learn.

They literally can't feel the signals.

When you wear diapers for years, your brain learns to tune out the sensation of peeing.

It becomes background noise. 

Something your brain stops paying attention to.

So when you ask a 4-year-old to "tell me when you need to go," they genuinely don't know.

Because they've spent four years in something that instantly absorbs everything.

They've never felt wet. Never felt uncomfortable.

Their brain learned to ignore that sensation completely.

This is why switching to pull-ups doesn't help.

Pull-ups absorb just as fast. They feel the same to the brain.

So the signal stays blocked.

And this is why older toddlers resist so hard.

They're being asked to notice something they've been trained to ignore.

Think of it like this.

We learn through cause and effect.

Touch hot stove -> Ouch, don't do again

Same thing applies here.

Their brain has no idea they have peed, they can't feel it

About how she'd say "I don't need to go" and then have an accident five minutes later.

She wasn't lying. She genuinely didn't feel it.

About how her brother trained so easily at 2 and a half.

He'd only been in diapers for two and a half years. 

His brain hadn't tuned it out yet.

But my daughter? Four years of diapers. Four years of her brain learning to ignore that signal.

No wonder nothing was working.

I wasn't asking her to learn something new.

I was asking her to unlearn four years of ignoring her body.

The next morning, I told my husband what I'd learned.

He said "that actually makes sense. So what do we do?"

I said we need to stop using diapers completely. And pull-ups won't work either.

We need something that creates strong enough sensory feedback that her brain can't ignore it.

He said "so just let her have accidents everywhere?"

I said no. There are training pants designed specifically for this.

Real training pants that let kids feel wetness but contain it.

I started looking.

Most training pants were either crap quality or not absorbent enough (complete mess).

But I kept seeing parents of older toddlers mention UpAiry training pants.

They said these had Feel & Learn technology. Strong sensory feedback but no leaking.

I read reviews from parents of 3, 4, even 5-year-olds who'd been stuck for years.

Same story over and over.

"My child couldn't feel anything in pull-ups."

"Once she could actually feel it, she got it in days."

"I didn't realize diapers had trained her brain to ignore the signal."

I was skeptical. We'd tried so many things.

But the science made sense.

And they had a 75-day guarantee.

After two years, I figured why not.

I ordered them.

When they arrived, I put them on my daughter.

"These are your new underwear. They work differently."

The first day, she had six accidents.

But something happened that never happened before.

Every single time, she stopped immediately.

"Mommy, it's happening."

Not "I went." Not "I'm wet."

"It's happening."

Present tense.

She could feel it while it was happening.

In four years, she'd never felt that.

Day two, five accidents. All announced as they happened.

Day three, she was playing. Stopped. Grabbed her stomach.

"Mommy, I feel something."

We ran to the bathroom. She went.

She looked amazed. "I felt it before!"

Week one, she started telling me before accidents.

Her brain was finally learning to recognize the signal.

Week two, she was making it to the potty most of the time.

Week three, two accidents all week.

My husband said "I can't believe the difference."

I said "she just needed to actually feel it."

Month two, she's been completely dry for three weeks.

Tells me when she needs to go. Takes herself sometimes.

Last week, I called the preschool. Asked about fall enrollment.

They said yes, there's still space.

She starts in the next few months.

Yesterday, she was playing outside with neighborhood kids.

Came inside once to use the bathroom. Went right back out.

No accidents. No issues.

On the way to bed, she said "I'm glad I learned."

And I realized something.

For two years, I thought she was resisting.

That something was wrong with her approach or my approach.

But she wasn't resisting anything.

Her brain just couldn't hear the signal.

And once I gave her something that created a signal strong enough to break through, she learned in weeks.

Look, if you have an older toddler who's been stuck for months or years, and nothing you've tried has worked, this might be why.

It's not behavioral. It's not stubbornness.

Years in diapers or pull-ups train the brain to tune out elimination signals.

You can try every method. Every reward. Every trick.

But if their brain can't hear the signal, they can't learn.

I spent two years trying everything except the one thing that actually mattered.

Sensory feedback.

These training pants worked because they create feedback strong enough that the brain can't ignore it anymore.

Not magic. Just science.

Here's the link if you want to check them out: https://www.upairy.com/pages/training-underwear

I'm not affiliated with them. 

Just a mom who finally figured out what was blocking progress.

My daughter's not in diapers anymore.

She's not stuck anymore.

And it only took weeks once we addressed the actual problem.

You don't need another method.

You need sensory feedback.

more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"My best friend's daughter potty trained in 3 days, while mine took over a year. Here's what we did differently...

Because when I look back at that year with my daughter, I realize I made it SO much harder than it needed to be.

My friend Melissa and I had our daughters three days apart.

We were pregnant together, went through labor at the same hospital, raised them side by side.

I thought "how hard can potty training be?"

I'd seen so many moms online do it in a weekend. Heck, there's even a method called "3 day potty training."

Oh boy was I wrong....

---

Last spring, Melissa and I decided to start potty training together.

We picked the same weekend. Made it fun. Did it side by side.

I bought the cute potty. I bought the sticker charts. And I stocked up on pull-ups because I HATE changing diapers and didn't want pee on my rugs.

And that was the decision that wasted over a year of our lives.

Day 3, Melissa texts me: "Mia went twice today! She's getting it!"

Day 3 for us? My daughter Lily had 10 accidents and screamed at the potty.

I texted back: "That's amazing! We're still figuring it out."

I figured okay, some kids are faster. Lily will get there.

Week two, Melissa: "She's basically got it. Maybe one accident a day."

Week two for us? Still 8-10 accidents daily.

I stopped updating her.

Month later, we met at the park.

Mia ran up and said "Mommy I need to potty."

They walked to the bathroom together. Done.

Lily had TWO accidents while we were there.

I watched Melissa's face. She was trying so hard not to look surprised.

On the drive home, I felt so defeated.

Same age. Same start time. Why did Mia train in days and Lily didn't train in months?

And I had no idea why.

---

So I kept trying. For a year.

Three-day method. Rewards. Timers every 20 minutes.

Nothing worked.

She'd say "I don't need to go" and pee two minutes later.

I thought she was stubborn. I thought she "wasn't ready."

Month eight, our pediatrician said "some kids just take longer."

But Mia didn't take longer.

Month eleven, I was exhausted. Buying pull-ups. Cleaning accidents. Feeling like I was failing.

---

So I was doom-scrolling Instagram one night, trying to unwind.

And I found a Reel from a Pediatric Therapist explaining the "Sensory Loop."

She asked a question that stopped me in my tracks: "How can you teach a child to control a sensation they literally cannot feel?"

She explained that modern disposables are engineering marvels. They absorb moisture so fast that the skin stays perfectly dry.

And that's when it hit me. That's why Lily said "No" when I asked if she was wet. She wasn't lying. She genuinely didn't feel it.

She went on to say: "You are trying to teach them to control a bladder they are deaf to."

She said the solution is to remove the disposables immediately.

BUT... she said do not use regular underwear either. Because while underwear helps them feel wet, it creates huge puddles on your floor.

And cleaning up accidents 5 times a day creates stress, which makes the child shut down.

So you are stuck:
Disposables = No Feeling (No Learning).
Underwear = Huge Mess (High Stress).

She said you need a hybrid - "Training Pants."

She recommended UpAiry training pants.

She said they have a specific technology that stays wet against the skin for just long enough to send a "signal" to the brain. It creates a sensory "Cause and Effect."

Pee = Wet. Wet = Yuck.

But the outer layer locks it in so it doesn't leak everywhere.

She also said this is why the last generation (our parents) never had the issues we have. They all used cloth diapers where the toddler COULD feel their mess.

She said she'd tried a few other brands out there but the UpAiry ones were the best she'd used.

It sounded too simple, but the logic made sense. So I ordered them.

---

Day 1 of using them: Lily peed. Stopped playing immediately. Looked down.

"Wet."

She felt it. The connection was instant.

With disposables, it took months for her to even notice she was peeing.

Day 2: She started to go, felt the dampness, and ran to the potty to finish. She realized she could STOP the "yuck" feeling by using the potty.

Day 3: She was dry most of the day. She went to the potty every time she felt the urge.

THREE. DAYS.

I looked at my husband and said, "Melissa's daughter trained in 3 days because she used something different. We struggled for a YEAR because of disposables?"

---

The next week, I asked Melissa what she'd used.

She said "Oh, I didn't use disposables. My sister told me they don't work because kids can't feel them. I used UpAiry training pants from day one."

I just stared at her.

That was the only difference.

Not her method. Not her kid.

What Mia was wearing let her feel wetness immediately.

What Lily was wearing erased the signal for a year.

When I got home I looked back through our texts and saw that she had originally sent me the link to UpAiry.

I ignored it and thought "We don't need those" 

🤦🤦🤦🤦

---

Also!!! I told three other moms I know who were struggling.

All were using disposables. All switched.

One texted me a week later: "Day 5. She's trained. I'm crying. Thank you."

Another: "He went from no awareness to fully trained in 10 days."

Third: "Why doesn't everyone know this?"

---

So if you're struggling with a toddler who won't train, and you've tried everything, check what they're wearing.

Training pants let them feel it immediately. That's what teaches them.

That's the difference between 3 days and a year.

Hope this saves another mom a year of stress.

more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"I've worked in early childhood education for 11 years.

I've helped potty train hundreds of kids across three different daycares.

And I can tell you something that most parenting books won't.

I can predict within the first week which kids are going to train fast and which ones are going to struggle for months.

It has nothing to do with the child's intelligence. 

It has nothing to do with their personality. 

And it has very little to do with the parents approach.

It has to do with one thing. 

And once I explain it, you'll probably look at your own child's situation completely differently.

—

Let me back up.

When I first started working in childcare, I assumed potty training was mostly about timing and temperament.

Some kids were ready at 2. Some weren't ready until 3 or later. Some were stubborn. Some were easygoing.

And for the first few years, I didn't question it.

But somewhere around year three or four, I started noticing a pattern that I couldn't explain.

We'd get a class of ten toddlers starting the potty training transition around the same age.

And without fail, the class would split into two groups.

Group one would show potty awareness pretty quick, and group two don't have a care in the world

You could ask them "did you just go?" and they'd say no.

Genuinely. 

They weren't lying and they weren't being difficult.

They had no idea.

And this group would struggle for months. Sometimes half a year. Sometimes longer.

I kept thinking it had to be a personality thing. Some kids just develop that awareness later.

But it wasn't consistent. I'd see a kid who was sharp as anything, sit in a wet pull-up for an hour without noticing. 

And I'd see a kid who was still barely talking, walk himself to the potty at 22 months like it was nothing.

It didn't track with development. It didn't track with temperament. It didn't track with anything I'd been trained on.

But it DID track with one thing.

What they were wearing when they arrived.

—

It took me years to put this together because I wasn't looking for it.
But once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it.

The kids who trained fast almost always came in wearing either cloth-style training pants or thin cotton underwear from day one.

The kids who struggled for months were almost always in disposables/diapers

Every. Single. Time.

I started paying closer attention. Not just to the kids in my class but across the entire center.

Same pattern.

Pull-ups and disposables = months of issues and zero awareness.

Cloth or cotton training pants = fast awareness and trained within weeks.

I brought this up to the center director once. 

She said "well yeah, kids in underwear feel it when they go, so they learn faster."

And I remember thinking... that's it? That's the whole thing?

Because if that's the whole thing, then why is everyone still putting their kids in disposables?

Why are we recommending them in our parent packets? 

If the thing they're wearing is the thing blocking the awareness, then aren't we actively making it harder?

—

There was a little girl in my class a couple years ago. I'm going to call her Sophie.

Sophie was 3 and a half. Smart. Social. One of the most verbal kids in the room. 

She could tell you about her weekend in full sentences. She knew every kid's name, every teacher's name.

But she could not potty train.

Her mom had been trying since Sophie turned 2. 

She was stressed. 

She'd pull me aside at least once a week.

"Any progress today?"

And I'd have to tell her no. Sophie had three, four, five accidents a day. 

I'd often walk over and say "Sophie, I think you might be wet."

She'd look at me confused. Then look down. Then say "Oh."

This went on for months.

Her mom tried everything. 

She brought special treats for rewards, every method and thing you've probably done yourself

Nothing changed.

Seeing Sophie say "I didn't go" when she obviously had.

And I kept thinking about the pattern I'd been seeing for years.

Sophie was in disposables every single day. 

Thick, absorbent, dry to the touch within seconds.

And she had zero awareness of her own body.

Those two things weren't a coincidence.

—

Around this same time, I started reading more about child development in toddlers. 

Not just the daycare training manual stuff — actual research.

There's a concept in child development called sensory filtering. 

It's the brain's ability to tune out repeated sensations so they don't distract you.

It's the same reason you stop noticing the feeling of your shirt on your skin after you put it on. 

Your brain filters it out. 

It's not useful information anymore so your brain stops paying attention to it.

When a baby pees in a diaper, the diaper absorbs it instantly. The skin stays dry. 

The brain gets no feedback.

So the brain learns: this sensation is irrelevant. Filter it out.

At 18 months, the filter is still weak. 

Most kids can still feel the signal if you take the diaper off.

That's why early training often works quickly.

But by 2 and a half, 3, 3 and a half — the filter is strong. Years of the brain practicing ignoring a signal that never produced any feedback.

Parents often put these kids in a classroom and ask them to tell us when they need to go.

But their brain is filtering the signal.

That's why Sophie would say "I didn't go" and genuinely mean it. 

Her brain had spent three and a half years erasing the sensation.

It wasn't anyones fault.

It was the product she'd been wearing since birth doing exactly what it was designed to do - keep her dry. 

This is also why our parents' generation trained earlier. In the 1950s, 92% of children trained by 18 months. 

Cloth diapers stayed wet. The brain always got the signal. The filter never built up.

Disposables removed the signal. The average training age nearly doubled.

And once I understood this, the pattern I'd been watching for years finally had a name.

Sensory erasure.

—

So here's what I did with Sophie.

I talked to her mom at pickup one day and told her everything I'd been observing.

I told her about the two groups I see and what they're wearing being the only consistent difference.

I told her about how the disposable were erasing the signal Sophie's brain needed to learn.

And I told her that she needed to get Sophie out of disposables and into training pants.

Real training pants. The kind that let the child feel wetness against the skin but contain it so there's no puddle on the floor.

She asked me which ones.

I told her the ones I'd seen work best with the kids in our center were UpAiry training pants. 

They have special layer that holds wetness against the skin long enough for the brain to register it, but the outer layer catches everything.

I'd seen other parents bring in different brands. 

Some leaked. 

Some were cheap polyester that irritated kids' skin.

The UpAiry ones were the only ones I'd consistently seen produce that awareness shift in the first few days.

She ordered them that night.

—

The next Monday, Sophie came in wearing them.

Around 10 AM she was at the art table painting. And she stopped. Brush in the air. Looked down.

"Miss? Pee pee."

Three and a half years old. Months in my classroom. She had NEVER said that. Not once.

I walked over and said "You're right, you are. Let's go get changed."

She looked at me and said "I didn't want to be wet."

She FELT something. And she didn't like it. And she told me about it.

That is the entire learning loop. 

Feel it → don't like it → communicate it → eventually learn to prevent it.

By the end of the first week, she was walking to the bathroom before most accidents. Not every time. But most.

Her mom came in on Friday and I said "She's telling us before she goes now."

She just stood there in the doorway. 

Didn't say anything for a second. Then said "Are you serious?"

Week two, Sophie was using the bathroom independently. 

Raising her hand, walking over, going. Coming back to the table.

Week three, not a single accident for three straight days. 

I wrote it in her daily report and her mom was SO happy 

She said "I've been trying for a year and a half. Thank you for telling me what was actually wrong."

But I didn't do anything special. 

Sophie did it by herself. 

All we did was stop blocking the signal it needed.

—

That was two years ago.

Since then I've had this same conversation with probably fifty parents. Maybe more.

It's always the same situation. Kid has been struggling for months. Parent has tried everything.

And every time I ask the same question: "What are they wearing during the day?"

And every time the answer is some sort of disposable.

And every time I explain what they are actually doing to the learning process and recommend they switch to UpAiry.

And almost every time, the parent comes back telling me things are finally clicking.

Because their child's brain finally had something to learn from.

—

Here's what I tell every parent who walks into my classroom.

If your child is 2 and a half or older and potty training isn't progressing, the first thing I'd look at is what they're wearing.

If they're in disposables during the day, their brain may not be getting the sensory feedback it needs to build awareness. 

Get them into training pants that let them feel wetness but contain it. 

That's the bridge between diapers and underwear that most parents skip.

The ones I've seen work consistently are UpAiry training pants. 

Here's the link: https://www.upairy.com/pages/training-underwear

I have zero affiliation with them. I just see what works in my classroom every day.

The pattern is always the same.

Sensory feedback = fast learning.

Sensory erasure = months of frustration.

It really is that simple.

Other kids his age are already done with this and we haven't even really started.

I keep telling myself we'll figure it out but honestly I have no idea what I'm doing anymore…

☝☝☝ That's what was running through my head 4 months ago. Not quite panicking, but definitely confused about how to even begin at this point…

—

So for the last year I kept telling myself "he'll do it when he's ready."

And every few months I'd try for a weekend and then give up when it didn't work.

I bought the potty seat, I read the books, I watched the videos.

But he'd refuse to sit on it or just didn't seem interested at all.

So I'd just put him back in diapers and tell myself we'll try again later.

And people would say "don't push him, he'll train when he's ready" and I believed them.

I thought I was being a good mom by not forcing anything.

So my nephew who's 11 months younger than my son got trained at 2 and a half.

And at every family gathering it's just obvious that my son is the only one still in diapers.

So my son started noticing too and asked why his cousin doesn't wear diapers anymore.

And I didn't really know what to tell him because honestly I didn't know why we couldn't figure this out either.

So last month we were at a playdate and one of the other kids pointed at my son's diaper and said "babies wear those."

And my son just looked down and didn't say anything but I could tell he felt something.

Like he's getting old enough to understand that other kids see diapers differently now.

So my mom called and gently asked if we'd started potty training yet.

And I had to admit we'd tried a few times but it never stuck and I didn't know what to do differently.

Like the concern in her voice made me realize this isn't just going to solve itself.

So that's when I realized I can't keep waiting and hoping this magically happens on its own.

And I started looking for help specifically for older toddlers who are still in diapers.

Like not advice for regular 2-year-olds, but for kids who are past 4 and still haven't started.

Someone who understands that I'm not being lazy, I'm just genuinely unsure what to do at this point.

So I found this child development specialist on Instagram who posted about "late starters."

And she had content specifically about the 4+ age group that most advice doesn't really address.

So I sent her a DM explaining my situation and that I'd been waiting for him to show interest.

So she asked me what I'd tried so far.

And I told her we'd attempted training a few times but he always resisted so we went back to diapers.

Like I didn't want to force him and make this a negative experience.

So she said "I'm going to tell you something that might be hard to hear and possibly controversial".

And I'm thinking oh no, what did I do wrong?

But then she said something that completely changed how I was thinking about this.

And it made me realize I wasn't "respecting his readiness" - I was just avoiding getting started.

So she explained that toddlers don't naturally "become ready" for potty training on their own.

Like she said imagine if we waited for kids to "be ready" to stop hitting or to share toys.

So we wouldn't do that because we understand they need to be taught these skills with guidance.

And potty training is the same - it's a skill we teach them, not something they just figure out alone.

So by waiting for him to "show interest," I was actually making it harder for both of us.

Because at 4 and a half, diapers are his normal and he has zero reason to change something that works perfectly fine for him.

And the longer kids stay in diapers, the more comfortable they get and the more they resist trying something new.

So that's why kids who train earlier often have an easier time — they haven't built years of diaper dependency yet.

Like at 2.5, diapers are familiar but not their entire bathroom routine for their whole life.

But at 4.5, he's been doing this one way for over four years straight.

And asking him to suddenly change that feels unnecessary and uncomfortable to him.

So this is why "waiting until they're interested" can backfire for older toddlers — they'll choose what's easy over what's new every single time.

Which is fair right? Even as an adult I really...really hate change or when I'm out of my routine.

You're essentially asking them to volunteer for something different when they have a perfectly comfortable system already.

And for kids past 3, this resistance only gets stronger as they get more set in their routine.

So she explained that older toddlers need a clear transition that removes the diaper as an option.

And the key is giving them the learning signal (feeling wet) without the chaos of regular underwear accidents everywhere.

But you can't use pull-ups because pull-ups feel exactly like diapers to them.

So the solution is training pants that create the "I'm wet" feeling but contain accidents during the learning phase.

Like they feel the wetness after they pee (that's the signal their brain needs) but it doesn't leak through to your floors.

And when there's no diaper option to fall back on, they adapt way faster than you'd think.

But she said, most training pants don't work well for older toddlers because they either feel like diapers or leak constantly.

You need ones designed to create a wet feeling strong enough that even a 4+ year old will notice and respond to it.

And I'm sitting there thinking... so I've been waiting for him to be "ready" but really I just needed to actually start the process?

I thought I was being patient but I was just putting this off?

"So what do I do now when we're already past 4?"

And she said the good news is older toddlers can actually train faster once you commit to starting.

Their brains are more developed so they understand cause-and-effect better than younger kids do.

So she recommended UpAiry training pants.

And they're designed with Feel & Learn technology that's strong enough for older toddlers to actually notice and respond to.

She said they are the best ones she's ever used, and I believe her as shes the expert.

Like younger kids might train in anything, but 4+ year olds need a stronger signal to break years of diaper habits.

So I ordered them thinking okay, we're really doing this now, no more putting it off.

And I told my son "you're getting so big, so we're learning to use the potty now like the other kids."

Like I didn't ask if he was ready, I just made it the new routine.

So the first 2 days were a little rough and he asked for his diapers back a few times.

Like he'd been comfortable for over three years and now suddenly things were different.

And I almost questioned if I should have waited longer because change is hard for him.

But day 3 something shifted and he stopped asking for diapers.

So he had 3 accidents but told me about each one immediately because he actually felt them.

And I realized the wet feeling was teaching him for me - I didn't have to constantly remind or nag.

But I was still cautious because we'd only been doing this for a few days.

Like what if he decides he wants diapers back next week?

But week two he started walking to the potty on his own without me suggesting it.

And one morning he woke up and said "I kept my underwear dry all night!"

So this was the first time he'd ever been aware of staying dry because he finally understood what wet actually felt like.

And week three my sister-in-law came over and noticed he was wearing training pants.

She seemed genuinely surprised that we'd made real progress this time as she'd seen first hand our struggle.

I could tell she thought this was just another "attempt" that wouldn't last.

And last weekend at a birthday party, another mom said "oh wow, you're out of diapers now?"

My son said "yeah I'm a big kid" with this proud look on his face.

Like he actually feels good about this change now instead of resisting it.

My husband said "I honestly didn't think we'd get here this year."

And I told him "we just needed to actually start instead of waiting for the perfect moment."

Also!!! Another mom from my neighborhood whose son is almost 4 messaged me after seeing us at the park.

She said her son is still in diapers too and she's been waiting for him to show interest but nothing's happening.

I sent her the link and told her "you just have to commit to starting and not have diapers as a backup."

Three weeks later she texted me saying her son trained in less than two weeks.

She said she wished she'd just started a year ago instead of waiting and waiting.

So if your child is older and still in diapers and you're not sure when or how to even begin or what to do...

Give these a go.

Because I am usually very skeptical about products that claim to work but all it took me is to actually commit and stop putting it off.

I hope my story helps someone out here!

And the longer kids stay in diapers, the more comfortable they get and the more they resist trying something new.

So that's why kids who train earlier often have an easier time — they haven't built years of diaper dependency yet.

Like at 2.5, diapers are familiar but not their entire bathroom routine for their whole life.

But at 4.5, he's been doing this one way for over four years straight.

And asking him to suddenly change that feels unnecessary and uncomfortable to him.

So this is why "waiting until they're interested" can backfire for older toddlers — they'll choose what's easy over what's new every single time.

Which is fair right? Even as an adult I really...really hate change or when I'm out of my routine.

You're essentially asking them to volunteer for something different when they have a perfectly comfortable system already.

And for kids past 3, this resistance only gets stronger as they get more set in their routine.

So she explained that older toddlers need a clear transition that removes the diaper as an option.

And the key is giving them the learning signal (feeling wet) without the chaos of regular underwear accidents everywhere.

But you can't use pull-ups because pull-ups feel exactly like diapers to them.

So the solution is training pants that create the "I'm wet" feeling but contain accidents during the learning phase.

Like they feel the wetness after they pee (that's the signal their brain needs) but it doesn't leak through to your floors.

And when there's no diaper option to fall back on, they adapt way faster than you'd think.

But she said, most training pants don't work well for older toddlers because they either feel like diapers or leak constantly.

You need ones designed to create a wet feeling strong enough that even a 4+ year old will notice and respond to it.

And I'm sitting there thinking... so I've been waiting for him to be "ready" but really I just needed to actually start the process?

I thought I was being patient but I was just putting this off?

"So what do I do now when we're already past 4?"

And she said the good news is older toddlers can actually train faster once you commit to starting.

Their brains are more developed so they understand cause-and-effect better than younger kids do.

So she recommended UpAiry training pants.

And they're designed with Feel & Learn technology that's strong enough for older toddlers to actually notice and respond to.

She said they are the best ones she's ever used, and I believe her as shes the expert.

Like younger kids might train in anything, but 4+ year olds need a stronger signal to break years of diaper habits.

So I ordered them thinking okay, we're really doing this now, no more putting it off.

And I told my son "you're getting so big, so we're learning to use the potty now like the other kids."

Like I didn't ask if he was ready, I just made it the new routine.

So the first 2 days were a little rough and he asked for his diapers back a few times.

Like he'd been comfortable for over three years and now suddenly things were different.

And I almost questioned if I should have waited longer because change is hard for him.

But day 3 something shifted and he stopped asking for diapers.

So he had 3 accidents but told me about each one immediately because he actually felt them.

And I realized the wet feeling was teaching him for me - I didn't have to constantly remind or nag.

But I was still cautious because we'd only been doing this for a few days.

Like what if he decides he wants diapers back next week?

But week two he started walking to the potty on his own without me suggesting it.

And one morning he woke up and said "I kept my underwear dry all night!"

So this was the first time he'd ever been aware of staying dry because he finally understood what wet actually felt like.

And week three my sister-in-law came over and noticed he was wearing training pants.

She seemed genuinely surprised that we'd made real progress this time as she'd seen first hand our struggle.

I could tell she thought this was just another "attempt" that wouldn't last.

And last weekend at a birthday party, another mom said "oh wow, you're out of diapers now?"

My son said "yeah I'm a big kid" with this proud look on his face.

Like he actually feels good about this change now instead of resisting it.

My husband said "I honestly didn't think we'd get here this year."

And I told him "we just needed to actually start instead of waiting for the perfect moment."

Also!!! Another mom from my neighborhood whose son is almost 4 messaged me after seeing us at the park.

She said her son is still in diapers too and she's been waiting for him to show interest but nothing's happening.

I sent her the link and told her "you just have to commit to starting and not have diapers as a backup."

Three weeks later she texted me saying her son trained in less than two weeks.

She said she wished she'd just started a year ago instead of waiting and waiting.

So if your child is older and still in diapers and you're not sure when or how to even begin or what to do...

Give these a go.

Because I am usually very skeptical about products that claim to work but all it took me is to actually commit and stop putting it off.

I hope my story helps someone out here!

I bought special "potty time only" books, added his favorite stuffed animals, even got one of those musical potties.

So I'd read book after book, do silly voices, anything to keep him there.

Like he knew where the potty was, he'd sit when asked, but that was it.

—

So one night after another accident-filled day I was scrolling Instagram feeling defeated.

And I saw a post from a pediatric occupational therapist about potty training resistance.

So I sent her a DM describing exactly what was happening.

She asked "what is he wearing during training?"

And I told her regular underwear at home, and I keep putting him on the potty every 20–30 minutes.

So she said "okay so here's what's actually happening" and I'm thinking finally, someone who gets this.

—

She said toddlers who sit but immediately get up aren't being defiant.

They genuinely don't feel the urge to go when they're sitting there.

Like imagine someone tells you to sit and "wait until you're hungry" but you just ate.

You’d sit for a few seconds, realize nothing is happening, and get up — because why would you stay?

And that's exactly what's happening with toddlers in regular underwear.

When you put them on the potty every 20–30 minutes, most of the time they don't actually need to go yet.

So they sit, feel nothing, and logically get up.

Then 10–15 minutes later their bladder fills up and they finally feel the urge.

But by that time they're off the potty, playing, and the accident happens.

So the real problem isn't that they won't sit — it's that they're sitting at the wrong times.

And you can't expect a 2 or 3 year old to sit still for 5–10 minutes "just in case" when their body isn't telling them anything.

Like adults wouldn't do that either — we go when we feel the need, not on a timer.

And regular underwear doesn’t create that awareness.

Week 2 — I realized I hadn't needed books, screens, songs, or bribery at all.

Both times we made it to the public restroom with no accidents.

My husband said "I can't believe we spent 4 months trying to keep him on the potty when he didn't even need to go."

And I said "yeah… we were solving the wrong problem this whole time."

—

Also!!! Another mom from my class messaged me after I mentioned this.

I sent her the link and said "stop the scheduled sits — let the training pants teach him what the urge feels like."

Two weeks later she sent me a voice message almost crying because it finally clicked for him too.

All he needed was to feel the sensation before he could act on it.

—

So if your toddler sits on the potty but won't stay there no matter what you try…

They're probably sitting when their body isn't telling them anything yet.

There’s real child psychology behind this, awareness comes before action.

And these training pants created the awareness my son needed.
