I know that sounds backwards, but every time you tape one onto your three-and-a-half-year-old, or tell yourself "she'll get it when she's ready," 

You might be using the one thing that's making it impossible for her to learn.

I used to do the same thing.

Asking "do you need to go potty?" twelve times a day and getting the same blank stare every single time.

Watching her pee in a diaper, then two minutes later ask to go to the bathroom to wash her hands. Like the connection just wasn't there.

Changing her right before we left the house. Getting to Target. Walking in. "Mama, I need a change." Every single time.

Going up a diaper size. Then another one. Watching her outgrow 4T clothes while still in overnight diapers during the day.

She turned four in March.

Four years old. Still in diapers. All day, every day.

My younger sister's kid trained at two and a half. My neighbor's twins trained at three. Every kid at the playground was in underwear except mine.

And the preschool I'd already paid the deposit for? They called six weeks before start date.

"We saw on the intake form that she's not fully trained yet. Our program requires—"

I cut her off. "She'll be ready. I promise. We're working on it."

But I didn't promise her. I begged her. Because I had no idea how I was going to make that happen in six weeks when we'd been trying for ten months.

We'd tried everything. The three-day method. Twice.

Both times ended the same way—day three, still having six accidents a day, me cleaning pee off the couch at 9pm then putting her back in diapers.

By day four because I physically couldn't keep doing it.

The sticker charts. The rewards. The potty watch that played a song every thirty minutes. The books where the characters go on the potty and everyone claps.

None of it worked.

She'd sit on the toilet for twenty minutes, get up, and pee on the floor five minutes later.

I bought the fancy wooden potty. The padded seat that goes on the big toilet. The step stool. The flushable wipes. The underwear with her favorite characters.

You name it, we've tried it...

She wore the underwear exactly once. Had three accidents in two hours. Looked at me and said, "I want my diaper back."

My husband asked one night, after I'd changed the sheets for the third time that week, "Is this normal? Should we be worried?"

I didn't know. 

I told him some kids just take longer. 

That's what everyone says, right?

She won't go to college in diapers. She'll get it when she's ready.

But she was four. 

And she wasn't getting it. 
And preschool started in six weeks. 
And I was changing twelve diapers a day on a kid who could write her own name and count to fifty.

I made an appointment with her pediatrician. Told her everything. She checked her over.

"Physically, everything's normal," she said. "Just keep being consistent. She'll get there."

But consistent with what? We'd been doing the same thing for ten months. 

If it was going to work, wouldn't it have worked by now?

I left that appointment and felt SO defeated.

Not because she said anything wrong. But because I'd hoped she'd tell me what I was doing wrong so I could fix it.

Two weeks later I was at a birthday party. Another mom mentioned her son had just trained. He was three and a half.

I asked her, trying to sound casual, "What did you end up doing that worked?"

She told me she's a pediatric occupational therapist and works with kids on developmental milestones all day.

Even she'd struggled with her own son until she understood what was actually blocking him.

She said most kids can't train in diapers because diapers are designed to pull wetness away from the skin.

They're supposed to keep kids dry. That's the whole point.

But kids learn by feeling wet. By not liking it. By their brain connecting "I peed" with "I feel uncomfortable now."

Diapers erase that entire signal. 

The absorbent core pulls the liquid away in seconds. 

Kids pee, stay dry, keep playing - their brain never makes the connection.

She said that's why so many potty training methods don't work.

For most toddlers, you're supposed to go straight to underwear, but then you're cleaning puddles off your floor eight times a day and it feels impossible. So you go back to diapers.

And then you're stuck. Because in diapers, they'll never feel the discomfort they need to learn.

She told me about training pants she'd used. Not diapers. Not regular underwear. Something in between.

They let kids feel the wetness—actually feel it against their skin—but had enough protection that accidents didn't destroy your furniture.

Her son had started telling her when he needed to go within four days. Not because of rewards. Not because of stickers. Just because he didn't want to feel wet.

The brand was UpAiry.

I ordered them that night. Six weeks until preschool. If they didn't work, I'd have to withdraw her and lose the deposit. But what else was I going to do?

Day one, I put them on her after breakfast. 10am, she had an accident. Stopped playing, looked down, pulled at the waistband.

"I'm wet," she said.

She'd never said that before. Not once. Not in ten months of accidents. She'd pee in a diaper and keep playing like nothing happened.

An hour later, she walked into the kitchen and said, "I need to go potty."

Ran to the bathroom. Pulled them down herself. Went.

I stood in the doorway staring at her.

Day two, three accidents. But she told me about all three. Felt them, didn't like them, came and found me.

Day three, two accidents. Both times she made it halfway to the bathroom before it happened.

Day four, she made it to the toilet every time except once during outside play.

Week two, we left the house in them. Target. The park. Playdate. She told me every single time.

Four weeks in, I bought regular underwear. But she still loves to wear her training pants.

She's been in underwear for two weeks now. She tells me when she needs to go. She goes by herself. She washes her hands after.

The box of diapers under her changing table is still sitting there. I keep thinking I should give them away. I know we won't go back to them but I'm scared ya know?

Preschool starts in one week. When they ask if she's fully trained, I get to say yes.

Not because I became more consistent. Not because she suddenly "got ready." Not because we found the right reward chart.

Because we stopped using the one thing that was preventing her from learning.

I'm not saying every kid who's still in diapers has the same problem.

But if you've been trying for months with no progress, or you're facing a preschool deadline, or you're watching other kids the same age move on while yours stays stuck—

Maybe it's not that they're not ready. Maybe it's that diapers are erasing the feedback they need to figure it out.

The training pants I used are called UpAiry. 

They're designed to let kids feel wetness without making you clean puddles off your floor six times a day.

My daughter puts them on herself every morning. That's it.

My name is Bec. I'm 31 years old.

"Our preschool room license doesn't allow for diapers," she said. 

"There's no changing table. We're not equipped for it."

Not move her. Kick her out.

I drove home trying not to cry.

Not half-heartedly. Really trying.

And I don't understand what we're doing wrong.

My best friend Sarah has a daughter the same age as Emma.

They were in the same infant room together. Born three weeks apart.

Six months ago, Sarah mentioned they were starting potty training.

I said, "Us too! How's it going?"

She said, "She's basically got it. Maybe one accident a day."

This was after one week.

One week.

Meanwhile, we were two months in and Emma was having 10 accidents a day.

I figured okay, some kids are faster. Emma will get there.

A month later, I asked Sarah how it was going.

"Oh, she's been fully trained for weeks now. It's so nice not buying diapers."

I just smiled. Didn't mention we were still stuck.

Three months after that, we're still buying diapers.

And now Emma's getting kicked out while Sarah's daughter has been trained for half a year.

Same age. Same start time. Completely different results.

I don't understand why.

When Emma turned 2 and a half, I did everything the books said.

Started with the child-led approach. 

Put a potty in the bathroom. Read her books about it. Made it positive.

The experts said she'd show interest when ready.

Day one was accidents everywhere. Expected.

Day two, she used the potty twice. I thought we were getting somewhere.

Day three, total shutdown. Wouldn't sit on it. Had a meltdown.

Back to diapers.

She'd use the potty once to get the reward. Then nothing for days.

I tried taking her every 30 minutes.

She'd sit there. Nothing.

Five minutes later, she'd pee in her diaper.

Nothing worked.

And I kept thinking about Sarah's daughter.

Why did it work for her in one week?

What was different?

"Why won't my toddler potty train."

She was talking about kids who have issues with potty training.

"When a child doesn't train after multiple methods, parents assume it's behavioral."

"But in most cases, it's not behavioral at all. It's sensory. The child literally cannot feel the signals their body is sending."

For most kids, by age 2 or 3, the signal is still strong enough to notice.

That's why the "typical" training age is 2 to 3.

But if a child doesn't train during that window?

The longer they stay in absorbent products, the weaker the signal gets.

By age 3, a child has spent three years learning to ignore that sensation.

Their brain has built a stronger and stronger filter.

"Child-led. Three-day. Rewards. Timers. If the child can't feel the urge to begin with, no method will succeed."

Then she said something that made everything click.

"Think about how we learn anything. We need feedback."

"Touch a hot stove, feel pain, learn not to touch it. With potty training, the feedback loop is: feel the urge, go to the potty, stay dry and comfortable." 

"But if they can't feel the urge? There's no feedback loop. There's nothing for their brain to learn from."

I sat there in the dark staring at my phone.

Emma would say "I don't need to go" and pee two minutes later.

She wasn't lying.

She genuinely couldn't feel it.

The rewards didn't work because she couldn't feel when to earn them.

The timer didn't work because she couldn't feel anything when she sat on t
he potty.

The child-led approach didn't work because she couldn't feel the signal that would make her "show interest."

"Real training pants hold wetness against the skin but contain it so you're not cleaning constant messes. That immediate feedback is critical."

We still have a week left on the 30-day deadline.

details","cards":[],"body":{"text":"I've worked in early childhood education for 11 years.

I've helped potty train hundreds of kids across three different daycares.

And I can tell you something that most parenting books won't.

I can predict within the first week which kids are going to train fast and which ones are going to struggle for months.

It has nothing to do with the child's intelligence. 

It has nothing to do with their personality. 

And it has very little to do with the parents approach.

It has to do with one thing. 

And once I explain it, you'll probably look at your own child's situation completely differently.

—

Let me back up.

When I first started working in childcare, I assumed potty training was mostly about timing and temperament.

Some kids were ready at 2. Some weren't ready until 3 or later. Some were stubborn. Some were easygoing.

And for the first few years, I didn't question it.

But somewhere around year three or four, I started noticing a pattern that I couldn't explain.

We'd get a class of ten toddlers starting the potty training transition around the same age.

And without fail, the class would split into two groups.

Group one would show potty awareness pretty quick, and group two don't have a care in the world

You could ask them "did you just go?" and they'd say no.

Genuinely. 

They weren't lying and they weren't being difficult.

They had no idea.

And this group would struggle for months. Sometimes half a year. Sometimes longer.

I kept thinking it had to be a personality thing. Some kids just develop that awareness later.

But it wasn't consistent. I'd see a kid who was sharp as anything, sit in a wet pull-up for an hour without noticing. 

And I'd see a kid who was still barely talking, walk himself to the potty at 22 months like it was nothing.

It didn't track with development. It didn't track with temperament. It didn't track with anything I'd been trained on.

But it DID track with one thing.

What they were wearing when they arrived.

—

It took me years to put this together because I wasn't looking for it.
But once I saw it, I couldn't unsee it.

The kids who trained fast almost always came in wearing either cloth-style training pants or thin cotton underwear from day one.

The kids who struggled for months were almost always in disposables/diapers

Every. Single. Time.

I started paying closer attention. Not just to the kids in my class but across the entire center.

Same pattern.

Pull-ups and disposables = months of issues and zero awareness.

Cloth or cotton training pants = fast awareness and trained within weeks.

I brought this up to the center director once. 

She said "well yeah, kids in underwear feel it when they go, so they learn faster."

And I remember thinking... that's it? That's the whole thing?

Because if that's the whole thing, then why is everyone still putting their kids in disposables?

Why are we recommending them in our parent packets? 

If the thing they're wearing is the thing blocking the awareness, then aren't we actively making it harder?

—

There was a little girl in my class a couple years ago. I'm going to call her Sophie.

Sophie was 3 and a half. Smart. Social. One of the most verbal kids in the room. 

She could tell you about her weekend in full sentences. She knew every kid's name, every teacher's name.

But she could not potty train.

Her mom had been trying since Sophie turned 2. 

She was stressed. 

She'd pull me aside at least once a week.

"Any progress today?"

And I'd have to tell her no. Sophie had three, four, five accidents a day. 

I'd often walk over and say "Sophie, I think you might be wet."

She'd look at me confused. Then look down. Then say "Oh."

This went on for months.

Her mom tried everything. 

She brought special treats for rewards, every method and thing you've probably done yourself

Nothing changed.

Seeing Sophie say "I didn't go" when she obviously had.

And I kept thinking about the pattern I'd been seeing for years.

Sophie was in disposables every single day. 

Thick, absorbent, dry to the touch within seconds.

And she had zero awareness of her own body.

Those two things weren't a coincidence.

—

Around this same time, I started reading more about child development in toddlers. 

Not just the daycare training manual stuff — actual research.

There's a concept in child development called sensory filtering. 

It's the brain's ability to tune out repeated sensations so they don't distract you.

It's the same reason you stop noticing the feeling of your shirt on your skin after you put it on. 

Your brain filters it out. 

It's not useful information anymore so your brain stops paying attention to it.

When a baby pees in a diaper, the diaper absorbs it instantly. The skin stays dry. 

The brain gets no feedback.

So the brain learns: this sensation is irrelevant. Filter it out.

At 18 months, the filter is still weak. 

Most kids can still feel the signal if you take the diaper off.

That's why early training often works quickly.

But by 2 and a half, 3, 3 and a half — the filter is strong. Years of the brain practicing ignoring a signal that never produced any feedback.

Parents often put these kids in a classroom and ask them to tell us when they need to go.

But their brain is filtering the signal.

That's why Sophie would say "I didn't go" and genuinely mean it. 

Her brain had spent three and a half years erasing the sensation.

It wasn't anyones fault.

It was the product she'd been wearing since birth doing exactly what it was designed to do - keep her dry. 

This is also why our parents' generation trained earlier. In the 1950s, 92% of children trained by 18 months. 

Cloth diapers stayed wet. The brain always got the signal. The filter never built up.

Disposables removed the signal. The average training age nearly doubled.

And once I understood this, the pattern I'd been watching for years finally had a name.

Sensory erasure.

—

So here's what I did with Sophie.

I talked to her mom at pickup one day and told her everything I'd been observing.

I told her about the two groups I see and what they're wearing being the only consistent difference.

I told her about how the disposable were erasing the signal Sophie's brain needed to learn.

And I told her that she needed to get Sophie out of disposables and into training pants.

Real training pants. The kind that let the child feel wetness against the skin but contain it so there's no puddle on the floor.

She asked me which ones.

I told her the ones I'd seen work best with the kids in our center were UpAiry training pants. 

They have special layer that holds wetness against the skin long enough for the brain to register it, but the outer layer catches everything.

I'd seen other parents bring in different brands. 

Some leaked. 

Some were cheap polyester that irritated kids' skin.

The UpAiry ones were the only ones I'd consistently seen produce that awareness shift in the first few days.

She ordered them that night.

—

The next Monday, Sophie came in wearing them.

Around 10 AM she was at the art table painting. And she stopped. Brush in the air. Looked down.

"Miss? Pee pee."

Three and a half years old. Months in my classroom. She had NEVER said that. Not once.

I walked over and said "You're right, you are. Let's go get changed."

She looked at me and said "I didn't want to be wet."

She FELT something. And she didn't like it. And she told me about it.

That is the entire learning loop. 

Feel it → don't like it → communicate it → eventually learn to prevent it.

By the end of the first week, she was walking to the bathroom before most accidents. Not every time. But most.

Her mom came in on Friday and I said "She's telling us before she goes now."

She just stood there in the doorway. 

Didn't say anything for a second. Then said "Are you serious?"

Week two, Sophie was using the bathroom independently. 

Raising her hand, walking over, going. Coming back to the table.

Week three, not a single accident for three straight days. 

I wrote it in her daily report and her mom was SO happy 

She said "I've been trying for a year and a half. Thank you for telling me what was actually wrong."

But I didn't do anything special. 

Sophie did it by herself. 

All we did was stop blocking the signal it needed.

—

That was two years ago.

Since then I've had this same conversation with probably fifty parents. Maybe more.

It's always the same situation. Kid has been struggling for months. Parent has tried everything.

And every time I ask the same question: "What are they wearing during the day?"

And every time the answer is some sort of disposable.

And every time I explain what they are actually doing to the learning process and recommend they switch to UpAiry.

And almost every time, the parent comes back telling me things are finally clicking.

Because their child's brain finally had something to learn from.

—

Here's what I tell every parent who walks into my classroom.

If your child is 2 and a half or older and potty training isn't progressing, the first thing I'd look at is what they're wearing.

If they're in disposables during the day, their brain may not be getting the sensory feedback it needs to build awareness. 

Get them into training pants that let them feel wetness but contain it. 

That's the bridge between diapers and underwear that most parents skip.

The ones I've seen work consistently are UpAiry training pants. 

Here's the link: https://www.upairy.com/pages/training-underwear

I have zero affiliation with them. I just see what works in my classroom every day.

In 11 years I've watched hundreds of kids go through this. 

The pattern is always the same.

Sensory feedback = fast learning.

Sensory erasure = months of frustration.

It really is that simple.

more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"F*CK POTTY TRAINING (respectfully).

Well here we are. Two and a half years old and first starting our potty training journey and it's not going great.

My mother-in-law came over yesterday and dropped the classic line: "You know, my kids were all trained by 18 months. I just sat you on the pot and you did it."

She looked at my son in a diaper like I was failing him.

I didn't think he was ready, but THE AMOUNT OF OUTSIDE PRESSURE drove me to do it.

It wasn't just her. It was my mom. My best friends. His teachers. And specifically that "Lululemon wearing ass" at the playground holding a Stanley cup.

Everybody made me feel like SHIT for NOT having my kid potty trained by now.

Like I’m doing something wrong because I can’t get him to do what apparently "everyone" did easily in the 90s.

But honestly? I think she’s remembering it wrong.

So I tried to follow her advice. I tried the timer. I tried the "just sit him down."

And this morning we hit rock bottom.

I put him on the potty right after waking up. He sat there for a full 2 minutes, not peeing, insisting he didn’t need to go.

I turn my back for literally 2 seconds and I hear "Uh-oh."

There he is, standing in a huge puddle on the hardwood floor. He stands in it just looking at it not giving a single f**k.

And then my 1.5-year-old rushes over and starts PLAYING IN IT.

I turn to grab the baby and I run into the wall. So now I’m trying to console one kid, keep the other out of the pee puddle, and I smell like urine.

AND it’s not even 8:00 am.

I was done. Checked out. I cannot live like this anymore.

--

So I was doom-scrolling Instagram while hiding in the bathroom (so I didn't scream).

And I came across this Reel from a child psychologist talking about "Gramnesia."

I didn't even know that was a word.

But she defined it as: "Grandparent Amnesia - when the older generation forgets how hard it actually was, or forgets that their circumstances were different."

So I sent her a DM explaining my MIL's comments and the disaster morning I just had.

And she said "Your MIL isn't lying, but she's leaving out a huge detail."

And what she explained next made me realize I wasn't crazy.

She said back then, most kids were in cloth diapers. When they peed, they felt wet immediately. It was gross. They WANTED to stop.

But today? We use super-absorbent disposables that wick moisture away in seconds.

So our kids literally never feel wet. They have zero incentive to use the potty because they are comfortable 24/7.

So when Grandma says "just put them on the potty"... She forgets that her kids had a biological signal (wetness) that my kid doesn't have.

She said "You are trying to teach a blind man to see color. He physically can't feel the signal."

And that’s why the timers and rewards aren't working — he doesn't feel the urge until it's on the floor.

But she said the solution isn't going back to 1980s cloth diapers and safety pins. It's using modern training pants that mimic that old-school sensation.

She said you need "feedback" pants that let them feel wet instantly, but still protect your floors.

So she recommended UpAiry training pants.

She said they have this specific Feel & Learn technology that replicates that "cloth diaper wetness."

So the child feels the consequence immediately, but the absorbent layer catches it so you aren't mopping up puddles.

She said she'd tried a few other brands out there but the UpAiry ones were the best she'd used.

And I'm thinking... so the problem wasn't me, and it wasn't my "stubborn" kid? It was just that he couldn't feel what was happening?

So I ordered them immediately. I told my MIL "we're trying something different."

--

Day 1 was rough, he had 2 accidents. But this time, he stopped dead in his tracks and looked down. "Momma Wet." He actually felt it!!!!

Day 3 he started to pee, felt the wetness, and stopped himself. He ran to the potty to finish.

Day 5 he went to the bathroom entirely on his own. No reminders. No battles.

Week 2 — he is dry all day.

And the best part? My MIL came over this weekend and saw him run to the potty by himself.

She said "See? I told you he just needed to focus."

I just smiled and didn't say a word. I know it wasn't "focus." It was the pants.

—

Also!!! I had been talking to another mom I met at the gym about this. Her son did the exact same thing - 2-second potty sits, accidents all day.

I sent her the link and said "let the training pants teach him what the urge feels like."

Two weeks later she sent me a voice message almost crying because it finally clicked for him too. All he needed was to feel the sensation before he could act on it.

—

So if your toddler is having serious potty issues or parents are making you feel like you're failing because "it was so easy" for them...

Ignore the noise.

There is actual child psychology to this, and our kids just need to feel the signal.

Hope this helps another mom who is smelling like pee today.
